tags.gist: Supports a risk-proportionate framework and calls the two axes a pragmatic start, but wants the paper to define what kind of risk assessment it means.
Warns the paper's initial regulatory assessment may be confused with product-specific risk assessment; only information reliably known at the start should feed the former.
Notes the ISO 14971 definition of risk overlaps the consequences axis, which some passages use more broadly, so the relationship needs defining.
Asks the paper to state at which level the term risk operates, calling the initial level criticality and keeping risk for ISO 14971.
Proposes two delineated phases: criticality stratification to set oversight and evidence, and product-specific risk management under ISO 14971 across the lifecycle.
Lists factors usable at stratification, from severity and autonomy to scope limits, user, reversibility, setting, time criticality, binding safeguards and traceability.
Would credit a safeguard at stratification only when it is a binding, enforceable part of the device or workflow, never an anticipated future control.
Suggests probability or evidence-certainty information could count at stratification where already supported, to fit requirements to a technology's maturity.
Would extend stratification to define the criticality profile and the constraints that hold the product within its level.
Wants stratification to reflect conservatively the highest criticality that cannot be excluded by enforceable constraints, using probability assumptions only when bounded.
Would make stratification reassessable when later development, clinical or postmarket information challenges its assumptions.
States the principle for Questions 2 to 6: a factor affects stratification only as a defined, assured property; others belong to product-specific risk management.
Agrees directiveness is a continuum and lists relevant aspects such as specificity, strength of recommendation, enforceable safeguards, time criticality and personalization.
Agrees the patient-facing distinction matters, but would base it on how reliably safeguards and independent review can be enforced in the setting, not the label.
Agrees the generalist-specialist distinction may be relevant, with caveats, and would base any effect on assurable competence and workflow rather than designation.
Would anchor stratification on the highest criticality reasonably foreseeable across conversational trajectories that safeguards cannot exclude.
Lists enforceable safeguards that could hold a conversation at a defined criticality, such as scope restrictions, refusal, mandatory handoff and oversight checkpoints.
Agrees the escalation errors are not commensurable; stratification can use their severity and built-in escalation procedures, but detailed weighting comes later.
Cautions against a binary view of escalation, since errors include wrong level, timing or destination along a graded spectrum.
Generally supports benchmarking plus clinical confirmation tailored to intended use and criticality, since exhaustive testing is infeasible.
Wants assumptions and safeguards that lower criticality or evidence burden, such as human review, themselves validated and fed back into the assessment.
Would use criticality, aligned with the two axes plus added aspects, to set evaluation extent, allowing staged reassessment as evidence develops.
Finds the clinician analogy useful but cautions against assuming equivalence, noting deskilling, and would treat human oversight as a control needing evaluation.
Asks the paper to distinguish output errors from their clinical consequences and clarify which each evaluation phase best addresses.
Proposes progressive deployment from a controlled envelope to expanded use through predetermined evidence gates, with rollback criteria and PCCP-like mechanisms.
Would expand benchmarking into a suite of representative, risk-enriched, subgroup, boundary and multi-turn assets with consequence-related metrics.
Says average performance must not offset poor results on critical subsets; wants prespecified floors for safety-critical failure modes.
Would develop simulated conversational trajectories into an explicit layer between static benchmarks and clinical confirmation, without replacing real users.
Wants benchmarking to test device-specific safeguards, and to consider independence and common-mode failure where one AI supervises another.
Suggests a prespecified regression suite on safety-critical competencies to show the impact of a foundation model change on the deployed configuration.
Would set clinical confirmation by criticality and residual uncertainty, favoring prospective evidence where human interaction matters and challenge testing for rare failures.
Wants retrospective evaluation to preserve temporal fidelity, withholding later findings from the device while allowing them in the reference standard.
Treats representativeness as multidimensional, separating evidence that estimates expected performance from evidence covering rare high-consequence situations.
Wants prespecified subgroup and failure-mode analyses, with sample sizes driven by the precision risk-based claims need rather than a uniform minimum.
Would scale clinical confirmation to criticality and residual uncertainty: prospective evidence where human interaction matters, challenge testing for rare failures.
Suggests proportionate local deployment qualification where safety depends on site conditions, stronger the more the regulatory case relies on them.
Would separate an independent reference standard from the comparator, which should be care without the device, judged by relative non-inferiority.
Would compare the intended user with and without the device against the same reference standard, with absolute criteria kept for critical safety outcomes.
Supports the approach while asking to strengthen it in six areas, from consequence-based evaluation and dynamic suites to relative comparison and lifecycle reassessment.
Supports the view that robust postmarket monitoring is especially important, including re-benchmarking, clinician review and degradation monitoring.
Wants monitoring to also check whether the assumptions and safeguards behind a device's criticality stay effective in real use.
Would extend postmarket evaluation beyond model performance to interaction, automation bias, team performance and clinical consequences, by criticality.
Notes device and environment co-evolve, so monitoring should reassess whether benchmarks, reference standards and deployment assumptions remain valid.
Wants monitoring tied to predefined metrics, triggers and actions such as rollback or restriction, on a timescale matching system change.
Accepts more postmarket reliance in principle but rejects a general trade-off that lets stronger monitoring automatically cut premarket evidence.
Lists considerations for acceptable premarket uncertainty: severity, reversibility, failure detectability, autonomy, exposure, ability to roll back and model stability.
Would let monitoring offset premarket uncertainty only when the residual uncertainty is observable, reversible and controllable.
Wants monitoring to verify that stratification assumptions, including effective human oversight and scope limits, still hold.
Supports the three approaches as complementary, not interchangeable, and would add team performance, near misses, overrides and outcomes by criticality.
Suggests dynamic postmarket evaluation with multi-turn scenarios and simulated or real interactions under changing deployment conditions.
Wants reassessment both periodic and triggered, listing triggers from adverse events and drift signals to guideline, workflow and foundation model changes.
Would monitor several forms of drift and ask whether the benchmark is still representative, not just whether the device still passes it.
Sees supervisory agents aiding scalable monitoring, provided a safety-relevant agent is itself validated and kept under surveillance.
Lists considerations for supervisory agents, with caution where device and supervisor share foundation models or architectures.
Would keep machine supervision as one layer, not a closed loop, with periodic human review especially for higher-criticality devices.
Welcomes stakeholder input but says distributed data collection must not distribute accountability; the manufacturer owns the strategy and corrective action.
Gives institutions a role in spotting deployment-environment changes and societies in guideline shifts, with defined interfaces and agreements.
Accepts the premarket baseline but would scale reassessment to a change's impact on competencies and safeguards, including cumulative small changes.
Wants post-change evaluation on retrospective cases to preserve temporal fidelity of the information available at decision time.
Would base GenAI PCCPs on procedural and boundary prespecification instead of specifying every modification technically in advance.
Would build staged progression from supervised use to independence into PCCPs, with downgrading when postmarket signals emerge.
Wants PCCPs to cover environmental changes that can invalidate prior assumptions even when the device is unchanged.
Would put foundation model change assessment in the monitoring strategy, with benchmarking and possible return to a supervised stage until evidence gates pass.
Asks for case-level reconstructability of the configuration in use, such as model version, prompts and guardrails, to investigate signals.
Frames monitoring as an active control system across the lifecycle whose permitted rate of change must match the ability to detect consequences.
Says agentic systems add system-level risks and make attributing and controlling failures harder when components come from different organizations.
Wants responsibility for the end-to-end system clearly assigned and backed by contractual, technical and quality arrangements, not diffused.
Wants premarket evaluation of representative end-to-end workflows, failure combinations and recovery, given error propagation across steps.
Calls for risk-based system-level testing of safety-relevant configurations, with integration-testing responsibilities clearly allocated.
Notes agentic systems need technical, semantic and governance interoperability, which grows harder when composition changes dynamically.
Wants stricter acceptance criteria as autonomy rises, including oversight checkpoints, failure containment and reverting to a safe state.
Concludes agentic AI needs end-to-end accountability, pathway-based evaluation and proportionate autonomy controls, not treatment as merely more capable GenAI.
Supports a risk-proportionate lifecycle approach that separates initial stratification from risk management and verifies the conditions for safe operation.
